transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
Outrage is growing over Cornell University's handling of an alleged gang rape in 2024.
There were Snapchat texts in which members of the CHI-5 fraternity invited other men
to join in.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul is calling for an independent investigation, NPR's Brian
Mann reports.
It was a busy fall day on campus, students heading to class, but Amoya mostly stopped
long enough to talk with me.
She said she was furious when she learned that some of the men involved were allowed
by Cornell University to write essays in order to reduce disciplinary action, and that's
outlined the lawsuit.
I feel like really disappointed in, I guess, Cornell.
I don't know how like a whole gang rape can be swept under the rug with essays.
They should be like in jail, not just expelled.
Those essays have really become a kind of symbol of what many students say was an inadequate
response by Cornell University.
NPR's Brian Mann reporting.
The man shot during an immigration enforcement action in Austin this month has been charged
with assaulting a federal officer.
Mo's Buchel from member station KUT reports ICE says a high-speed chase led up to the
shooting.
In early accounts from his legal team, Wilbur Garcesperes said he did not know he was being
pursued by immigration agents before he was shot.
A criminal complaint filed by ICE says officers identified themselves during an initial stop
before he fled in his car, hitting one of them with a side-view mirror.
That led to a chase and ended with one agent forcing a stop, then shooting Garcesperes,
saying he feared he'd be struck by the car.
The criminal complaint says one of the two officers was wearing a body camera for the
initial stop, but that the agent turned the camera off before arriving at the scene of
the shooting.
But Garcesperes has filed a federal lawsuit, primarily seeking to block deportation.
I'm Mo's Buchel in Austin.
The Trump administration ban on about one billion dollars worth of Canadian goods took
effect today, Dan Karpanchuk reports.
The main items include some alcoholic beverages, dairy and motorcycles.
President Trump's decision to go ahead with the ban will likely ratchet up trade tensions
even further, as the White House punishes Ottawa for retaliating earlier this month to
previous additional tariffs against Canada.
Experts say the ban isn't economically significant in the nearly one trillion dollars worth of
trade between the two countries.
Trump has already expressed confidence that his latest moves would force Ottawa to come
back to the negotiating table with an apology, and a trade deal would come in three to four
weeks.
Canada has not indicated yet whether there would be further retaliation, and the trade
standoff could continue for months.
For NPR News, I'm Dan Karpanchuk in Toronto.
President Trump says the government won't limit the development of A.I., even as top
tech executives have called for delays.
A.I. executives had lunch with Trump at the White House today.
Trump says the leaders signed a voluntary accord calling on them to "self-police"
the technology.
This is NPR News.
Congress has passed a bill to formally end the production of pennies after 233 years.
It gives a legal stamp of approval to President Trump's decision to stop producing the currency
that penny was among the first coins to be made after the U.S. Mint was established in
1792.
The union, representing 8,000 EPA employees nationwide, has filed a lawsuit over the agency's
termination of their union contract last year from member station GBH.
Craig Lamolt has more.
The EPA terminated its union contract last summer after President Trump signed an executive
order ending collective bargaining rights for more than a million federal employees.
Lily Simmons heads AFGE Local 3428, which represents EPA employees in New England.
She says those workers have lost protections that were in the contract.
For example, you go out and you do some water sampling, and it's bad.
And you need to share that bad news, and you need to make sure that people are not using
that water as a source of drinking water.
But are you going to lose your job for saying so?
That is a real concern for people.
The executive order cited national security concerns.
The EPA has not responded to a request for comment.
For NPR News, I'm Craig Lamolt in Boston.
Invasive Burmese pythons in the Florida Everglades are adapting to their new environment.
They're now climbing trees.
The pythons were imported to Florida through the exotic pet trade.
Now tens of thousands of the giant constrictors have decimated native wildlife populations.
According to the Palm Beach Post, they're now climbing cypresses and live oaks to bask
in the sun during colder months.
listening to NPR News from Washington.

Man shot during ICE immigration enforcement action in Austin charged with assaulting federal officer
Trump administration ban on approximately one billion dollars of Canadian goods takes effect today
President Trump meets with tech executives, says government won't limit artificial intelligence development
Congress passes bill to formally end penny production after 233 years of U.S. currency
EPA union files lawsuit over agency's termination of union contract for 8,000 employees nationwide
Invasive Burmese pythons in Florida Everglades adapt by climbing trees to bask in sun
